events.title: Massacre of the Constantinian princes
events.summary: In the summer of 337 the army at Constantinople murdered Constantine's half-brothers Julius Constantius and Flavius Dalmatius, his nephews the Caesar Dalmatius and Hannibalianus ('King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples'), the patrician Optatus and the prefect Ablabius, leaving only Constantine's three sons and two small boys, Gallus and Julian.
events.detail: The soldiers claimed they would accept only Constantine's sons. Julian later blamed Constantius II directly; Eusebius and Christian writers present it as the army's spontaneous will. On 9 September 337 Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans were proclaimed Augusti, and in 338 they met in Pannonia (Viminacium) to divide the empire: Constantine II the West beyond the Alps, Constans Italy, Africa and Illyricum, Constantius the East.
scholarship: Burgess, 'The summer of blood: the Great Massacre of 337', DOP 62 (2008)
events.debate: Constantius II's degree of responsibility is debated; Burgess argues he organised it.

events.title: First siege of Nisibis by Shapur II
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis for some 63 or 70 days; the city held, its defence later credited by Syriac tradition to the prayers of Bishop Jacob of Nisibis, who reportedly sent a plague of gnats against the Persian elephants.
events.detail: The Syriac poet Ephrem, a deacon of Nisibis, wrote hymns (Carmina Nisibena) on the three sieges. Jacob's role and the gnats belong to hagiography; the siege date may be 337 or 338.

battle.significance: Opened 25 years of Persian attempts on Roman Mesopotamia.

events.title: Constantine II killed invading Italy
events.summary: Constantine II, claiming seniority and resentful of his share, invaded Constans' territory and was ambushed and killed near Aquileia (at the river Alsa) in spring 340; Constans took over the whole West.

events.title: Ulfilas consecrated bishop of the Goths
events.summary: Ulfilas (Wulfila), a Goth descended from Cappadocian captives of the 250s raids, was consecrated 'bishop of the Christians in the Getic land' by Eusebius of Nicomedia, probably at the Dedication Council of Antioch; he devised a Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible, omitting, it was said, the Books of Kings as too warlike.
events.detail: Expelled in a persecution by the Tervingian leadership around 347-348, he settled with his flock near Nicopolis ad Istrum. His Homoian theology made 'Arian' Christianity the faith of the Goths, Vandals and other Germanic peoples, a confessional divide with Nicene Romans that shaped the post-Roman kingdoms. The Codex Argenteus in Uppsala preserves much of his Gospel text.
scholarship: Heather and Matthews, The Goths in the Fourth Century (1991)

events.title: Constans' winter crossing to Britain
events.summary: Constans crossed the Channel from Boulogne in midwinter 343, an unusual feat celebrated by Firmicus Maternus, apparently to deal with trouble on the northern frontier involving the areani (frontier scouts) or with Picts and Scots.

events.title: Council of Serdica
events.summary: Called by Constans and Constantius to settle the Athanasian dispute, the council split on arrival: about 90 western bishops under Ossius met in Serdica, restored Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra and gave the bishop of Rome a right to hear appeals, while some 80 eastern bishops withdrew to Philippopolis and excommunicated Julius of Rome and Ossius.
events.detail: The schism of East and West over doctrine and authority, preceded by the eastern Dedication Council of Antioch (341) with its four creeds, made the Trinitarian question a lever in relations between the imperial brothers; Constans threatened war to restore Athanasius, who returned to Alexandria in 346.

events.title: Shapur II's persecution of Christians
events.summary: Shapur II imposed a double tax on Christians and, when Catholicos Simeon bar Sabba'e of Seleucia-Ctesiphon refused to collect it, had him executed with many clergy at Karka d-Ledan, beginning a 'Great Persecution' in Persia that lasted intermittently until Shapur's death in 379.
events.detail: Persian Christians were suspected as a fifth column after Constantine's conversion and his letter to Shapur claiming protection of them. The Syriac Acts of the Persian Martyrs record thousands of victims, a number modern scholars treat with caution.

sources.w: Acts of the Persian Martyrs (Martyrdom of Simeon)

scholarship: Smith, Constantine and the Captive Christians of Persia (2016)

events.title: Night battle of Singara
events.summary: Constantius II's army stormed Shapur's camp near Singara and appeared victorious, but in the disordered night fighting the Persians counterattacked and inflicted heavy losses; Shapur's heir Narseh was captured and killed.
events.detail: Julian's panegyric presents it as a Roman victory spoiled by indiscipline; Festus and Ammianus' allusions treat it as a defeat. Ammianus says Constantius fought nine major battles against Persia without a decisive success.

battle.significance: Bloodiest battle of Constantius' Persian war; neither side gained ground.

events.title: The Chronograph of 354
events.summary: The calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus produced an illustrated almanac for a wealthy Christian Roman, Valentinus, combining the pagan festival calendar, consular fasti, a list of popes, the earliest list of Christian feasts (Depositio Martyrum, including 25 December as Christ's birth), a city chronicle and the regionary catalogue of Rome.
events.detail: It illustrates the easy coexistence of pagan and Christian culture among the Roman elite in the mid-fourth century and is a fundamental source for chronology and topography.

events.title: Third siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis for about four months (his second attempt had failed in 346), damming the Mygdonius river and releasing the floodwater against the walls, which partly collapsed; the defenders under Lucillianus built a new wall behind the breach overnight and repelled the attack with Persian elephants bogged in mud.
events.detail: Ephrem and Julian's panegyric describe the flooding vividly. News of nomad attacks on his eastern frontier forced Shapur to withdraw, freeing Constantius to march west against Magnentius.

sides.strength: royal army with elephants and Indian contingents

battle.significance: Nisibis' successful defence preserved Roman Mesopotamia until 363.

events.title: Usurpation of Magnentius and death of Constans
events.summary: At a birthday banquet at Augustodunum, the comes Flavius Magnentius, of part-Frankish or British origin, appeared in purple and was acclaimed emperor by officers alienated from the unpopular Constans, who fled and was killed by Gaiso near Helena (Elne) in the Pyrenees.
events.detail: Magnentius, though probably pagan-tolerant, used the chi-rho as a large reverse type on his bronzes (with alpha and omega), possibly the first use of a Christian symbol as the sole design of a coin. He controlled Gaul, Britain, Spain, Africa and Italy.

events.title: Vetranio and Nepotianus
events.summary: On 1 March 350 the old general Vetranio was proclaimed in Illyricum, apparently at the instigation of Constantina, sister of Constantius, to block Magnentius; in June Constantine's nephew Nepotianus seized Rome with gladiators for 28 days before Magnentius' officer Marcellinus killed him and massacred his supporters. Vetranio abdicated before Constantius' army at Naissus on 25 December 350 and retired to Prusa.

events.title: Battle of Mursa
events.summary: Constantius II defeated Magnentius on the Drava near Mursa in one of the bloodiest battles in Roman history: Zonaras reports 24,000 of Constantius' 80,000 and 30,000 of Magnentius' 36,000 killed. Constantius' heavily armoured cavalry (cataphracts and clibanarii) turned Magnentius' left.
events.detail: Eutropius judged that the losses weakened Roman manpower for foreign wars; Constantius spent the battle in a martyr's shrine with the Homoian bishop Valens of Mursa, who announced victory as revealed by an angel. Magnentius fled to Aquileia and then Gaul. The general Silvanus defected with his troops to Constantius before the battle.

battle.significance: Decided the civil war; remembered as a catastrophic bleeding of Roman military manpower.

events.debate: Casualty figures from Zonaras are probably exaggerated.

events.title: Battle of Mons Seleucus and death of Magnentius
events.summary: After Constantius forced the Alpine passes, Magnentius was defeated at Mons Seleucus in the Cottian Alps; abandoned by his troops, he killed his family and committed suicide at Lugdunum on 10 August 353, and his brother Decentius hanged himself at Senones.
events.detail: Constantius' notary Paulus 'Catena' ('the Chain') then conducted savage treason trials in Britain, described by Ammianus.

events.title: Execution of the Caesar Gallus
events.summary: Constantius Gallus, Caesar at Antioch since 351, ruled by terror (Ammianus' extant narrative opens with his excesses, including a lynching of the governor of Syria during a famine); summoned west, he was arrested and beheaded near Pola.

events.title: Usurpation of Silvanus at Cologne
events.summary: Silvanus, Frankish magister militum in Gaul, framed by a forged letter at court, proclaimed himself emperor at Cologne; after 28 days he was murdered in a chapel by soldiers suborned by Ursicinus, whose staff included Ammianus Marcellinus.
events.detail: Ammianus, an eyewitness participant, gives the court intrigue in detail. The Franks then sacked Cologne in the confusion.

events.title: Julian made Caesar and sent to Gaul
events.summary: Constantius summoned his last male relative, the philosophy student Julian, from Athens, married him to his sister Helena and proclaimed him Caesar at Milan, sending him to Gaul with a small force and close supervision.
events.detail: Ammianus records Julian muttering a line of Homer about 'purple death' as he was robed. Julian had been secretly initiated into Neoplatonic theurgy by Maximus of Ephesus around 351.

events.title: Constantius II visits Rome
events.summary: Constantius entered Rome on 28 April 357 for his vicennalia in a triumphal adventus, motionless in his carriage 'as if a statue'; he admired the Forum of Trajan, erected the obelisk of Thutmose III (now the Lateran obelisk) in the Circus Maximus and removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house.
events.detail: Ammianus' description is a classic set-piece of late Roman imperial ceremony and of senatorial Rome's self-image.

events.title: Battle of Argentoratum (Strasbourg)
events.summary: Julian, with 13,000 men, defeated an Alamannic coalition of seven kings under Chnodomar, perhaps 35,000 strong, near Strasbourg; 243 Romans and 4 tribunes fell against some 6,000 Alamanni killed on the field and many more drowned in the Rhine. Chnodomar was captured.
events.detail: Ammianus' account, the most detailed of any late Roman battle, describes the Roman cavalry breaking before the Alamannic infantry until Julian rallied them in person, and the Batavi and Reges and the Cornuti and Bracchiati units holding the line with the barritus war cry. The army acclaimed Julian Augustus on the field, which he refused. The victory secured the Rhine and made Julian's reputation.

sides.losses: 6,000 killed on the field, many more drowned

battle.significance: The most complete late Roman battle narrative; restored the Rhine frontier.

events.debate: Ammianus, an admirer of Julian, may minimise Roman losses and inflate enemy numbers.

events.title: Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia and the Homoian creed
events.summary: Constantius convened twin councils, some 400 western bishops at Ariminum and about 160 eastern at Seleucia in Isauria; under pressure, both accepted a creed saying the Son was 'like (homoios) the Father according to the Scriptures', banning the term ousia. A council at Constantinople ratified it in January 360.
events.detail: Jerome's famous line, 'the whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian', refers to this settlement. The Homoian creed, preceded by the 'Blasphemy of Sirmium' of 357, was the official faith of the eastern empire until 378 and of Ulfilas' Goths.

events.title: Siege of Amida
events.summary: Shapur II, invading with allied Chionites under King Grumbates and guided by the Roman defector Antoninus, besieged Amida for 73 days; Ammianus Marcellinus, inside the city, describes the death of Grumbates' son before the walls, siege towers, sallies by Gallic legionaries, plague and the final storming via a collapsed siege mound.
events.detail: Seven legions and other troops were trapped in the city; the garrison commander Aelianus and tribunes were crucified, and Ammianus escaped through a postern by night. The delay cost Shapur the campaigning season. Ammianus' account (books 18-19) is one of the great eyewitness siege narratives of antiquity.

sides.strength: 100,000 (Ammianus) with Chionite, Albanian, Segestani allies and elephants
seven legions and citizens, c. 20,000 in the city (Ammianus)
sides.losses: city stormed; garrison killed or captured

battle.significance: Persian victory, but costly delay that saved the rest of Mesopotamia that year.

scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Kelly, Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian (2008)

events.title: Siege of Singara
events.summary: Shapur took Singara with a ram that broke a newly repaired stretch of wall, deporting its garrison, legions I Flavia and I Parthica, and the inhabitants to Persia.

sides.strength: legions I Flavia and I Parthica, cavalry and citizens

battle.significance: Loss of a key Roman base in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Sieges of Bezabde
events.summary: Shapur stormed Bezabde on the Tigris, defended by three legions (II Flavia, II Armeniaca and II Parthica), and garrisoned it; Constantius' autumn counter-siege failed in the rains.

battle.significance: Persia gained a bridgehead in the Transtigritane regions ceded in 299.

events.title: Julian proclaimed Augustus at Paris
events.summary: Ordered to send his best auxiliary units east for the Persian war, Julian's troops at Lutetia, many recruited on the promise of never serving beyond the Alps, mutinied and raised him on a shield as Augustus, crowning him with a soldier's torque in place of a diadem.
events.detail: Julian claimed he had been forced. Negotiations with Constantius failed, and in 361 Julian marched east down the Danube with remarkable speed, his men sailing from Raetia to Sirmium, while Constantius moved west from Antioch. Aquileia held out for Constantius.

events.title: Death of Constantius II at Mopsucrenae
events.summary: Marching against Julian, Constantius died of fever at Mopsucrenae in Cilicia aged 44, reportedly naming Julian his successor on his deathbed after being baptised by the Homoian bishop Euzoius; civil war was averted.

events.title: Julian's restoration of paganism
events.summary: Sole emperor from December 361, Julian reopened temples and restored sacrifices, recalled exiled bishops of all factions (to let Christians quarrel, Ammianus says), purged the palace staff, and tried to create a pagan priestly hierarchy imitating Christian charity.
events.detail: His edict of 17 June 362 required teachers to be approved by city councils, and a circular explained that Christians could not honestly teach Homer and Hesiod while despising their gods; Ammianus, a pagan admirer, condemned it as harsh, 'to be buried in eternal silence'. Julian wrote treatises Against the Galilaeans and hymns to King Helios and the Mother of the Gods. Christian sources (Gregory of Nazianzus' invectives) cast him as 'the Apostate'.

events.title: Julian at Antioch: the Daphne fire and the Misopogon
events.summary: Wintering at Antioch, Julian alienated the Christian and pleasure-loving city with his sacrifices, his beard and price controls during a grain shortage; when the temple of Apollo at Daphne burned on 22 October 362, he blamed Christians and closed the cathedral. Lampooned by the Antiochenes, he replied with the satirical Misopogon ('Beard-Hater').
events.detail: Julian had ordered the removal of the relics of the martyr Babylas from Apollo's sanctuary, and the fire followed the translation of the relics.

events.title: Julian's attempt to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem
events.summary: Julian ordered the Jewish Temple rebuilt under the supervision of Alypius of Antioch, to falsify Christian prophecy; Ammianus reports that 'fearful balls of fire' burst from the foundations, burning workmen, and the project was abandoned, probably also because of the earthquake of 19 May 363 and Julian's death.
events.debate: Cause of the fires (gas in cisterns, earthquake, miracle in Christian accounts).

events.title: Siege of Maiozamalcha
events.summary: Marching down the Euphrates, Julian took the fortress-town of Pirisabora and then stormed Maiozamalcha near Ctesiphon by mining under the walls, Roman soldiers emerging inside a house while the defenders watched the assault on the walls.

events.title: Battle of Ctesiphon (363)
events.summary: Julian's army made a night crossing of the Tigris under fire and defeated the Persian army under the Surena before the walls of Ctesiphon, killing 2,500 for about 70 Roman losses (Ammianus); but Julian judged the city too strong to besiege.
events.detail: Julian then burned his river fleet of over 1,000 ships, so that the 20,000 men needed to haul it upstream could fight, and struck inland toward the Persian interior hoping to meet Procopius' northern army, a decision Ammianus and later writers regarded as fatal.

battle.significance: Tactical victory that brought no strategic result.

events.title: Battle near Samarra and death of Julian
events.summary: Retreating north up the Tigris under constant Persian harassment, Julian rushed into a skirmish without his breastplate and was struck by a cavalry spear that pierced his liver; he died that night in his tent, discussing the soul with the philosophers Maximus and Priscus.
events.detail: The killer was never identified: Libanius suggested a Christian Roman soldier, while Persian and other sources credit a Persian or Saracen. The Christian legend has Julian cry 'You have won, Galilean'. His death left the army stranded deep in enemy territory; the next day the officers chose Jovian, a Christian guards officer.
events.locName: Near Samarra (Toummara/Maranga region), on the Tigris

sides.losses: significant, incl. generals Merena and Nohodares (Ammianus)

battle.significance: Death of the last pagan emperor; ended the Constantinian dynasty and forced the peace of 363.

events.debate: Identity of the killer; site of the battle.

events.title: Jovian's peace with Shapur II
events.summary: Trapped without supplies near Dura on the Tigris, Jovian accepted a thirty-year peace ceding five Transtigritane regions, Nisibis, Singara and Castra Maurorum, and abandoning Rome's alliance with Armenia; the citizens of Nisibis were evacuated, weeping, to Amida.
events.detail: Ammianus, who marched in the retreat, calls it a shameful peace without precedent in Roman history. Ephrem the Syrian left Nisibis for Edessa. The treaty created the frontier that lasted, with modifications, until the sixth century, and exposed Armenia to Persian conquest.
scholarship: Lightfoot, 'Facts and fiction: the third siege of Nisibis', Historia 37 (1988)

events.title: Death of Jovian at Dadastana
events.summary: Jovian died on his way to Constantinople at Dadastana on the Bithynian-Galatian border, apparently from charcoal fumes from a brazier in a freshly plastered bedroom, after a reign of eight months in which he restored Christian privileges.
